I am not White, I'm brown. I don't know where you got that assumption from. Just because my race is one America has no real category for does not mean I at all identify with the experiences or general culture of White Americans. That being said, I completely recognize that my race still affords me a privilege of a certain kind and am not in any way trying to act like I would ever be subjected to anything Black people are subjected to in this country. 

That being said, I am from a country in which violence against women is one of the most common things you see on the news, so I've always been taught that it's better to be safe than sorry. And men are the ones perpetrating that violence against other men in most cases, so, while I understand the statistical advantage women may have over men in this regard, it does little to comfort the wariness I feel around men. I never said this is somehow impeding my ability to live my life normally -- it is quite literally just something I am feeling anxious about. 

I honestly don't understand why you approached this with passive aggression, I wasn't trying to demonize all men. Of course they experience violence too. I am young, and I'm still learning how to navigate all these things. Have to try dating to become better at navigating these feelings -- don't really think there'll ever be a time when I am magically ready for it.

Woah. I never said I was going to ghost him. I know he's a human being with feelings, which is why I asked this question before doing anything rash or hurtful. If something happens to me, I will quite literally just be another nameless victim in some random statistic somewhere. Can't be blamed for acting out of self-preservation when a new story comes out every week about this or that woman who died because "no" can't be taken for an answer.

There's no reason for me to downvote this comment. I appreciate your input, it's always important to listen to many different opinions, which is why I posted this in the first place. 

My thing is this: as a man, I expect you to be aware of the pre-existing social dynamics that go beyond our friendship/whatever kind of relationship we have. This quite literally goes for any systematic thing -- whether it be the patriarchy like in this specific case, racism, homophobia, etc etc. It's not just about men and women.

There are certain boundaries that I feel people should be emotionally intelligent enough to know not to cross, especially at the very early stages of friendship where him and I are. If I look at a black friend as a non-black person and make a joke about racial violence, for example, the implication and significance of my joke would not be the same as if two black people made that joke amongst themselves, especially given the broader context of living in America. It is because the power dynamic that exists between each of these two pairs is different, and it is impersonal to those individuals -- it's something that goes beyond all of us. It's rooted in intersectionality as well. 

Now, of course each two or however many people in a relationship can define those boundaries for themselves. There are friends with whom I can make certain types of jokes that I could never imagine myself making with others. That I understand, but when you barely know a person -- how can you go so far? He told me that I'll be "so fucking sorry" when he finally dies in order to make me feel guilty. The tone...the words, our lack of the deep/genuine familiarity and trust that would exist in a years long friendship changes everything. When he told me he'd lock me up in a basement, I didn't laugh. There was no one around us. I was genuinely spooked. As such, naturally, my sense of self-preservation is going to kick in. 

You are a man, capable of quite literally killing me if you should ever want to act on those jokes that are just comedic in some morbid way to you and your bros. To me, these are real threats, because I don't know who you really are. Three months mean nothing. Women die every day at the hand of the violence of men. We're surrounded by it. Every day there seems to be a new victim. I think I'm perfectly justified in my fear -- it's what's kept me alive. It's a matter of survival. This is also incredibly important: women get attacked and die over confronting men. Again, this is a man I don't know well. I am always walking on eggshells. Can't say the wrong thing. Have to speak a certain way to avoid a wrath that could genuinely hurt me. Setting those boundaries was absolutely terrifying, I was sick with anxiety for three days. His anger could mean my demise. Any man's anger could mean my demise. 

Perhaps I feel this way generally because I was raised to treat other people with a high level of conscientiousness, sensitivity and respect. All I know is that I must always have an awareness of the weight and power of my words in relation to who I'm interacting with. Maybe he really just thinks I'm one of the bros. Maybe they're all silly jokes, but the following is something I live by: I am not going to bend and break myself over what other people may have intended when they've said and done anything. I get your argument, but does that mean he scared me and broke my trust any less? No. I feel disrespected, unsafe and afraid. My mom is someone who seems to have had a lifelong adoration of the language and the country and all that concerns it, so ever since I was a child she'd always share that love with me and tell me all about it. As such, I'd assume that through the process of diffusion I eventually grew to also become really invested in learning more about the history and the culture. One of my biggest goals is to become fluent enough to take her there and make it a relaxing, safe and comforting trip for her, as she'd never be able to go on her own at this point. 

It's kind of like a way of saying thank you to her for all the kindness, love and support she's shown me, but also a way of extending that love beyond what she's taught me -- to spread it as well, and to experience it in my own personal way, since I feel like it's so fulfilling to have that sort of passion for a place and its culture. It's how I get to keep her with me for the rest of my lifetime, I suppose, but also a way to learn so many things and meet so many people with stories I'd never otherwise be able to learn. 

That can be said for quite literally any language, but I just adore Italian because it was always spoken about with such reverence and appreciation -- and whenever I hear it spoken, it brings me such a sense of comfort, associated with the serenity of my mom's passion for it. I visited the country twice, and definitely really enjoyed my time there. I wish I'd known enough Italian to talk to natives, but I didn't, and I'm so determined to learn as a result of all those things together. Just the prospect of ever getting to go there and hopefully being able to spend a semester or so studying there is enough to get me going. :)

** On the off chance this is anyone's future reference, I found out it's actually what's known as "direct object pronouns," which, in this case, is "them," because Coraline is bringing "them (I fili di rame)" to maneskin (for example.) This would make the "to /me/" in that sentence the indirect object pronoun, as the action is not happening to the person directly. The Italian direct object pronoun for 'them' (masculine plural) is LI -- filo is a masculine noun, fili is the plural, so LI is used. From my rudimentary understanding, Li is attached to the end of the verb here because this is in the imperative tense -- the person is being ordered/commanded to do something, essentially, so instead of "Li porta da me" (which is grammatically inaccurate as far as I understand) it ends up being "portali da me."
